Which was to be demonstrated.

### Corollary
From this, given the law of resistance and the difference *Aa* between the arcs *Ca* and *CB*, the proportion of the resistance to gravity can be found very nearly.

For if the resistance *DK* is uniform, the figure *BKTa* will be a rectangle under *Ba* and *DK*; and hence the rectangle under 1/2 *Ba* and *Aa* will be equal to the rectangle under *Ba* and *DK*, and *DK* will be equal to 1/2 *Aa*. Wherefore, since *DK* is the <term>exponent</term> <gloss>indicator or representative measure</gloss> of resistance, and the length of the pendulum is the exponent of gravity, the resistance will be to gravity as 1/2 *Aa* is to the length of the pendulum; exactly as was demonstrated in Proposition 28.

If the resistance is as the velocity, the figure *BKTa* will be very nearly an ellipse. For if a body, in a non-resisting medium, should describe the length *BA* in a complete oscillation, the velocity in any place *D* would be as the <term>ordinate</term> <gloss>the vertical coordinate of a point in a geometric figure</gloss> *DE* applied to the diameter *AB* of the circle. Hence, since *Ba* in a resisting medium, and *BA* in a non-resisting medium, are described in approximately equal times; and therefore the velocities at each point of *Ba* itself are very nearly to the velocities at the corresponding points of the length *BA* as *Ba* is to *BA*; the velocity at point *D* in a resisting medium will be as the ordinate applied to the circle or ellipse described on the diameter *Ba*; and therefore the figure *BKVT a* will be an ellipse very nearly. Since the resistance is assumed proportional to the velocity, let *OV* be the exponent of the resistance at the middle point *O*; and the ellipse *BRVSa*, described with center *O* and semi-axes *OB*, *OV*, will be very nearly equal to the figure *BKVT a*, and the rectangle under *Aa* and *BO* equal to it. Therefore, the rectangle under *Aa* and *BO* is to the rectangle under *OV* and *BO* as the area of this ellipse is to the rectangle under *OV* and *BO*: that is, *Aa* is to *OV* as the area of the semi-circle is to the square of the radius, or as 11 to 7 approximately: And therefore 7/11 of *Aa* is to the length of the pendulum as the resistance of the oscillating body in *O* is to its gravity.

But if the resistance *DK* is in the <term>duplicate ratio</term> <gloss>the ratio of the squares</gloss> of the velocity, the figure *BKVT a* will be almost a parabola having its vertex at *V* and its axis *OV*, and therefore will be very nearly equal to the rectangle under 2/3 *Ba* and *OV*. Therefore, the rectangle under 1/2 *Ba* and *Aa* is equal to the rectangle under 2/3 *Ba* and *OV*, and thus *OV* is equal to 3/4 *Aa*: and therefore the resistance of the oscillating body at *O* is to its gravity as 3/4 *Aa* is to the length of the pendulum.

<summary>Newton provides a corollary for calculating the ratio of resistance to gravity in a pendulum's swing. He derives specific geometric proportions for cases where resistance is constant, proportional to velocity, or proportional to the square of velocity.</summary>

# ON BIRD-CATCHING
<note>original: "DE AVCVPIO"</note>

<meta>continues from previous page: Hold the membrane from a dog’s afterbirth, or a hare’s fur</meta> or its dung, or those who carry the <term>peristereon</term> <gloss>vervain</gloss> herb. A black stone like a bean is found in the Nile; upon seeing it, dogs do not bark. You shall carry a dog's tongue in your shoe, placed under the big toe, or if you carry a dried dog's heart with you, according to Sextus <note>Sextus Placitus, a late Roman medical author</note>. Or hare's hair, or dung, according to Pliny <note>Gaius Plinius Secundus, the Roman natural historian</note>. Or you shall carry the severed tail of a young weasel on your foot, or give the dog a frog in a morsel of food; all these things serve to avoid the barking of dogs. Nigidius <note>Publius Nigidius Figulus, a Roman scholar and contemporary of Cicero</note> says that dogs flee the sight of anyone for a whole day who has pulled a tick from a pig and carried it for a short while. Oppian <note>A 2nd-century Greco-Roman poet who wrote on hunting and fishing</note> wrote:

> If you carry a small piece cut from the skin of a hyena,
> Both fierce puppies and dogs will be struck
> With sharp terror; they will not bark at you
> As you walk hereafter, even if they barked before.

### That a dog cannot run.

Smear its wings <note>original: "alas," which usually means wings, but in the context of a dog likely refers to the armpits or the "wings" of the shoulder</note> with oil, for it will be hindered in its course; it will happen in this manner.

### That a hawk be spirited.

You shall encourage the bird against its prey so that it attacks large birds. Soak the bait used during hunting time in wine. Or, if it is a goshawk <note>original: "astur"</note>, give it a little vinegar. When you wish it to fly, give it three morsels of meat soaked in wine, or pour wine into a pigeon's beak from your own mouth and then make the hawk fly. Thus:

### You will make partridges more inclined to fight,

If you give them small branches of <term>adiantum</term> <gloss>maidenhair fern</gloss> to eat, according to Pliny. And:

### Roosters become more inclined to fight,

By giving them garlic in their food when they are about to fight. For this reason, in ancient comedy, they are very wittily called <term>eskorodismenoi</term> <gloss>garlicked</gloss> <note>original Greek: ἐσκοροδισμένοι</note>, which means "fed with garlic," to describe one who is vehement and too inclined to a fight.

### Lest a bird fly high,

Pull out the tail feathers that direct the course upward; thus it will fly in a circle below. If you wish:

### That a bird cannot fly,

Cut the upper and lower nerves of the wing; it remains without harm, but the bird will not fly. In this way, they do not escape from aviaries.

<summary>This page details various charms and natural remedies to control animal behavior, including ways to silence dogs, increase the aggression of hawks and roosters, and prevent birds from flying away.</summary>
<keywords>animal husbandry, hunting dogs, falconry, folk medicine, Pliny the Elder, Oppian, garlic, avian management</keywords>

While walking, the aforementioned **Neptune** showed me, hidden beneath a certain rock, two minerals of that island: **Gold** <note>original: *Auri*</note> and **Steel** <note>original: *Chalybis*; in alchemical theory, iron or steel is often described as the "magnet" that attracts the celestial influence of the sun into the metallic body.</note>. Not far from there, I was led to a meadow in which a special Garden was planted with various trees most worthy of being seen. Among these many trees, he showed me seven trees distinguished by names <note>These represent the seven metals of antiquity, which were linked to the seven planets.</note>; among these, I observed two principal ones more eminent than the others. One of these bore fruit like a most bright and shining **Sun** <note>original: *Solis*</note>, and its leaves were like **Gold**. The other, indeed, produced very white fruits, whiter than lilies, and its leaves were like fine **Silver** <note>original: *Argentum*</note>. These trees were called by Neptune: one the **Solar Tree** <note>original: *Solaris Arbor*</note>, and the other the **Lunar Tree** <note>original: *Lunaris*</note>.

And although on this island everything was at their beck and call, yet one thing alone was missing. Water was not to be had, except with great difficulty. There were indeed many who attempted to lead spring water <note>original: *Aquam Fontis*</note> there through channels; others also extracted it from various substances; but the labor attempted was in vain, because it could be obtained by no means in that place. Even if it was obtained, it was nevertheless useless and poisonous, unless it was drawn from the rays of the Sun or the Moon, which few were able to perform; and whoever had favorable fortune in accomplishing this was never able to attract more than ten parts <note>In alchemical practice, "parts" denote the specific ratios or measures of a substance required for the Work.</note>.

For that water was of a marvelous kind; and believe me, I saw with my own eyes and felt with my hands the snowy whiteness of that water, and while I contemplated that water, I was greatly changed. It is as if the truth were perceived through the eyes of reason; and by the confidence of his belief, he stands as far above other men as the sun surpasses the other stars with its light. For the sun himself illuminates the other stars not so much by the magnitude of his power as by his divinity and holiness. Believe this sun to be a second god, O Asclepius, who governs all other things and illuminates all worldly beings, whether they possess souls or are inanimate. 

For if the world is a <term>living being</term> <gloss>original: animal mundus</gloss> that lives forever—and has been, and is, and will be—then nothing in the world is mortal. In every single part of a living being that exists in the world, as in one and the same ever-living organism, there is no place for death. Therefore, God himself must be most full of life and eternity, if it is necessary for him to live forever. 

Just as the world is everlasting, so the sun itself is forever the governor of living things, or the one who constantly attends to and dispenses all their vitality. God, therefore, is the everlasting governor of the living beings, or the vital things, that are in the world, and he is the eternal dispenser of life itself. He distributed it once by an eternal law, providing life to all vital things, in the manner I shall now describe.

<summary>This page describes the pious man's excellence through solar imagery and defines the sun as a second god that governs all life. It argues that because the world is an eternally living being, no part of it can truly be subject to mortality.</summary>
<keywords>sun as deity, cosmic vitality, immortality of the world, Asclepius, divine governance, piety, life dispenser, world organism</keywords>

# Solutions to the arguments.
</margin>

It is clear regarding the first argument. There is no doubt that just as, by God's permission, men can be killed, so too can that member or others be removed truly and realistically. But in such cases, demons do not operate through the witches of whom mention is now made. And through this, the solution to the second argument is also clear. But as for the point that because God permits the generative power to be more bewitched on account of [certain reasons], therefore it is also permitted that the member be truly and realistically removed—this is not valid as a general rule. This would not be done by way of witchcraft, nor do witches even desire this when they perform such works, for they do not wish to lack the power of restoring the member when they want and know how. From this, it is clear that it is removed not truly, but by a <term>prestigiosa arte</term> <gloss>glamorous art or the art of illusion</gloss>.

Regarding the third argument, concerning the transformation of Lot's wife <note>Genesis 19:26</note>: we say that it was a true transformation and not done by glamorous art; however, we are now speaking of glamorous art. Regarding the fourth: that demons can induce certain <term>formas substantiales</term> <gloss>substantial forms</gloss>, and therefore can also remove them. It is said regarding the magicians of Pharaoh that they created true serpents, and demons can produce certain effects concerning some <term>imperfectas creaturas</term> <gloss>lower animals or simple organisms</gloss> with the aid of some other agent, which they cannot do concerning men, for whom God has greater care. According to the text: "Does God care for oxen?" <note>1 Corinthians 9:9; the authors imply God's providence is specifically focused on humanity</note>. They can, however, always harm men truly and realistically or even by glamorous art if God permits it, as has been said; and by this, the solution to the last argument is also clear.

### Third Article: Whether more universal things are prior in our intellectual knowledge.

Ad tertium sic proceditur. It seems that more universal things are not prior in our intellectual knowledge: because those things that are prior and better known according to nature are posterior and less known according to us; but universals are prior according to the nature of our intellect. Furthermore, composite things are prior as far as we are concerned, and simple things [are later]; but universals are [simpler, therefore] known later as far as we are concerned. Furthermore, the Philosopher <note>Aristotle</note> says in the first book of the *Physics* that the definition falls first into our knowledge, and the parts of the definition are less universal: just as "animal" is a part of the definition of "man"; and universals are known later as far as we are concerned. Furthermore, we arrive [at causes] through effects and [from consequences to] principles; but universals are known later as far as we are concerned.

On the contrary is what is said in the first book of the *Physics*, that one must proceed from universals to singulars.

I respond that it must be said that in the knowledge of our intellect two things must be considered. First, indeed, that intellectual knowledge in some way takes its beginning from sensitive knowledge. And because sense is of singulars, while the intellect is of universals, it is necessary that the knowledge of singulars as far as we are concerned be prior to the knowledge of universals. Second, it must be considered that our intellect proceeds from <term>potentia</term> <gloss>potency/possibility</gloss> to <term>actus</term> <gloss>act/actuality</gloss>. And whatever proceeds from potency into act first arrives at an incomplete act, which is the middle between potency and act, and then a perfect act. Now, the perfect act to which the intellect arrives is complete science <note>original: "scia", meaning certain knowledge</note>, through which things are known distinctly and determinately; however, the incomplete act is imperfect science, through which things are known indistinctly under a certain confusion. For that which is known in this way is known both in act and in a certain way in potency. As it is said in the first book of the *Physics*: things that are more confused are first manifest and certain to us; but later we know by distinguishing the principles and elements distinctly. It is manifest, however, that to know something in which many things are contained, without having proper knowledge of each of those contained in it, is to know something under a certain confusion. In this way, both the universal whole, in which the parts are contained in potency, and the integral whole can be known; for each whole can be known in a certain confusion without the parts being distinctly known. To know distinctly that which is contained in the whole is to have knowledge of a less common thing: such as to know "animal" indistinctly, and to know animal in which there is "rational" or "irrational," which is to know "man" or "lion." Therefore, knowing "animal" occurs to our intellect before knowing "man." And the same reasoning falls if we compare any more [universal] to a less [universal], just as the sense goes out from potency into act, so does the intellect; and that order

Those things which make up a single ray in the light of the world make up myriads in the light of heaven. In the light of heaven, intelligence and wisdom are present. It is that light which flows into the light of the world in the external or natural man, and enables him to perceive the objects of things through the senses. If that light did not flow in, man would never have any perception, for the life within the things of the world's light comes from that source. From these things conclude that it is necessary to proceed according to my prescription, and not at all according to yours. Here there is a need for you to follow me, not for me to follow you. Rather, this must be the goal: that through alchemy the <term>arcana</term> <gloss>medicinal secrets or hidden virtues</gloss> may be detected, and the seductions of the <term>seplasiariorum</term> <gloss>perfume-sellers or ointment-peddlers; a derogatory term for pharmacists</gloss> may be exposed. For by these men the crude common folk are deceived, as they provide for one florin that which they would not redeem for a single penny. So "precious" are their secrets.

<margin>Poison is also in the best things.</margin>
Who is he who would dare to deny that even in the best things poison lies hidden and exists? All are forced to confess this. If this therefore is true, I now ask of you: is not the poison to be separated from the good and the useful? Must not the good be received and the evil left behind? Indeed, truly, it must be so. If therefore it must, I pray you, relate to me how that separation is performed in your shops? For among you all things remain mixed together. Yet to protect your simple-mindedness, if you are forced to confess that poison is hidden there and are asked where it eventually goes, you then bring forth I know not what regarding "corrections," which you claim drive out and take away the poison. 
<margin>The correction of the Physicians is examined.</margin>
Just as they say Quince corrects <term>Scammony</term> <gloss>a harsh purgative plant resin</gloss>, or as <term>Diagridium</term> <gloss>a prepared form of scammony</gloss> is said to be corrected. But what kind of correction is that? Does the poison not remain afterward just as it was at first? And yet you meanwhile boast that you have corrected it, so that the poison no longer harms. Where, then, did it escape? 
<margin>Diagridium.</margin>
It remains in the <term>Diagridium</term>. Test it, if you are wise: exceed the proper measure, and you will see where the poison is. For you shall know it quite quickly. Thus you also correct <term>Turbith</term> <gloss>a purgative root</gloss> and call it <term>Diaturbith</term>. Your "corrections" are of the sort that would befit peasants and should be given to pack-horses. Make a trial by exceeding the measure and increase the dose: you will see if you do not feel the poison. 
<margin>What "I, a Physician, correct" means.</margin>
*To correct is to take the corrected substance.* If a man is malicious and has sinned, and he is punished <note>original: "plectitur", meaning beaten or penalized</note>, the correction lasts no longer than the will of the one who was punished. Such are these pharmaceutical corrections: the power remains with the substance, not with you. Now truly, in this case, a Physician should consider nothing more than that the poison be removed. This ought to be done through separation. As an example: a serpent is poisonous, yet it is adopted as food. If you take away the poison from it, you may eat it with no harm. The same is to be understood equally concerning all other things; there is a similar need for separation. Until that is done, you cannot be secure in your operation, unless by chance nature supplies your deficiency, or a greater benevolence of the heavens favors you. For in your own art, no protection will remain.

Now therefore, at last, let us look at that true foundation which takes away poison, and how Alchemy provides it. This must be done in such a way that if <term>Mars</term> <gloss>iron</gloss> is in the <term>Sun</term> <gloss>gold</gloss>, the Mars may be removed; and if <term>Saturn</term> <gloss>lead</gloss> is turned in <term>Venus</term> <gloss>copper</gloss>, it may be separated from her. For as many ascendants and impressions as there are in the things of nature, so many bodies also exist within them. But where those bodies are contrary, it is necessary that one be taken away and removed, so that in this way all contrariety may be lifted, and the evil which you seek to avoid may be removed from the good. 
<margin>Fire perfects all things.</margin>
Just as gold is useful for nothing unless it is first cast into the fire, so a Medicine is much less useful if it does not pass through the fire. For it is necessary that all things pass through fire into a second generation, which ought to benefit and help man. Should this not rightly be considered the honest foundation of any Physician? For a Physician ought to apply not poisons, but <term>arcana</term>. 
<margin>The shops are rebuked.</margin>
But all those official preparations in the shops, as many as they are, do not contribute even a single letter to this doctrine. Instead, they are simply occupied in "correcting," as if a dog farts in a room <note>original: "pepedit"</note>, and that stench is suppressed either by lozenges and incense, or by juniper wood. I ask you: does not the stench remain in the room just as much after as before? And although it is not perceived by smell, can anyone therefore say the stench has been separated and remains no longer? On the contrary, it is present, but merely corrected by the perfume. Thus the perfume and the stench enter the nostrils together. Of this kind also are the corrections of the Pharmacists, who dull an <term>Aleopaticum</term> <gloss>a bitter medicine containing aloes</gloss> with sugar so that it may seemingly inflict no harm.
